column4: The section's dictionary form صراط (ṣirāṭ) is the walked road; this verse calls God's way a straight path, commands following it, and contrasts it with plural ways that divide travelers from it.

The source section's صراط الذين أنعمت عليهم (“the path of those You favored”) is named again here: those favored are prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous, and they are good companions on the way.
As the prompt's example indicates, ضل سواء السبيل directly makes straying a loss of the road's middle; the context warns against exchanging faith for disbelief.
The section's dictionary form “middle of the road” is made explicit by سواء الصراط; the disputants ask for guidance to the path's center while warning against excess.
The section's dictionary sense of هدى is showing someone a way; Moses, traveling toward Midian, asks God to guide him to سواء السبيل, the middle of the way.
The section asks to be led on a straight path; here revelation guides followers of God's good pleasure through سبل السلام and then to a straight path.
The section's lost traveler is staged directly: a man is حيران in the land while companions call him إلى الهدى; their call contrasts with the devils' diversion.
The source image is a road walked by feet; this verse contrasts someone walking fallen on his face with one walking upright on a straight path.
This verse places people on every road to threaten travelers, block God's way, and seek عوجا (crookedness); it reverses the section's open, straight communal road.
The verse contrasts taking سبيل الرشد with taking سبيل الغي; it makes the section's straight path and its opposite into two chosen routes.
The section's path is a community's traveled way; the Prophet calls it “my way” (سبيلي), and says he and his followers call people to God with insight.
The section's hidaya includes a guide leading someone on a way; Abraham tells his father to follow him and promises to guide him to صراطا سويا, an even path.
After naming earlier prophets, the verse says God guided them and commands the Prophet to follow their guidance; it concretely supplies predecessors whose path can be followed.
The section pictures a path belonging to a favored community; this verse warns against opposing the Messenger and following a path other than that of the believers.
The verse joins holding fast to God with being guided إلى صراط مستقيم, linking continued adherence to arrival on the straight path.
The section's dictionary definition of hidaya names both road and destination; God calls people to دار السلام and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
The people of the Garden say “He guided us to this”; their arrival at a destination through divine guidance makes the section's road-to-home gloss concrete.
Here the source section's root ع ب د retains its Quranic sense: “worship Me” is directly identified as a straight path, as in the section's worship-and-road sequence.
The section notes that worship and the walked road remain distinct senses in one word family; this verse explicitly places worship of God beside “this is a straight path.”
As in the section's root link between ع ب د and the road, Jesus commands worship and identifies it as a straight path.
This verse repeats the section's precise conjunction: God is Lord, so worship Him; that worship is called a straight path.
After listing prophets and their kin, the verse says God chose and guided them to a straight path; it links a community and its lineage to the traveled way.
The Prophet is told to say his Lord guided him to a straight path, a sound religion; the verse brings guidance, the path, and dīn together as the section does.
“This is your Lord's straight path” is followed by the claim that signs have been made clear; this ties the road to the signs by which it is recognized.
The verse says God placed roads in the earth لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ, so physical routes and being guided are joined as in the section's image.
The section's dictionary form for ع ل م includes a mark used to find a road; here عَلامات and stars are explicit means by which people find their way.
Stars are made as signs by which people find their way through land and sea darkness; this is the same navigation-by-signs relation developed from ع ل م in the section.
This verse asks who guides people in the darknesses of land and sea and who sends winds as good tidings; it makes guidance a concrete problem of navigation.
God spreads the earth and makes roads through it; the section's path is likewise a walkable ground that carries travelers toward where they are going.
The earth is made a resting place and roads are placed in it لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ; this directly parallels the section's paths made for finding one's way.
God places mountain passes and roads so people may find their way; this gives the section's navigable path a specific landscape and purpose.
The earth is made a spread-out surface so people can travel its broad roads; this closely stages the section's walked, passable road.
The section's dictionary form الطريق المعبد describes a subdued, easy-to-travel road; the bee is told اسلكي سبل ربك ذللا, to take its Lord's ways made yielding/easy.
Iblis says he will lie in wait on God's straight path; the verse makes the road itself the site of opposition to those who follow it.
The verse continues Iblis's ambush from front, back, right, and left; these approaches show opposition surrounding the straight route named in 7:16.
The section ends with guidance and the straight path; here the gathered wrongdoers are led to صراط الجحيم, the same guiding action and path with an inverted destination.
After the command to worship on a straight path in 36:61, this verse says Satan led many astray; it names the road's opposite as being misled.

This command tells the criminals to separate on Judgment Day; 36:60–62 then contrasts their separation with worship on the straight path and Satan's diversion, while this verse contributes the separation.
The command not to worship Satan because he is an enemy leads into 36:61's identification of worship as the straight path; this verse contributes the specific rival object of worship.
The verse says the aimed way belongs to God, while some ways are crooked; that is a direct road-level contrast to the section's straight path.
Breaking oaths can make a foot slip after it was firm and turn people from God's way; this concretely reverses the stable, well-trodden road in the section.
God's guidance is followed, and its follower will neither go astray nor suffer; this gives the section's request for guidance a promised consequence.
God shows the human the way, then the person is either grateful or ungrateful; the verse makes the guided road a point of choice, as the section's path contrasts the guided and straying.
The verse says God showed the human the two high roads (النجدين); this presents the section's straight path against an alternative route.
The verse describes people who استقاموا على الطريقة, staying upright on the way; it directly matches the section's third hidaya sense of continuing without leaving the path.
The command to hold fast to revelation is followed by “you are on a straight path”; it makes staying with guidance an act of remaining on the road.
The Prophet is described as guiding to صراط مستقيم; this directly joins the section's guide who goes before with the route he leads people toward.
The verse says believers were guided to good speech and to the path of the Praiseworthy; it supplies a specific destination on the path.
God guides those who believe to a straight path; this is another direct formulation of the section's requested route.
The Prophet calls people to a straight path; this directly stages a caller showing others the route.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path after sending clear signs; the verse joins discernible signs to finding the route.
Obedience to God and the Messenger is followed by guidance to a straight path; it depicts how one comes to walk the road.
The verse says God will guide the Prophet to صراطا مستقيما; it is a direct statement of the guidance requested in the section.
After promising gains and protection, the verse says God will guide the believers to a straight path; it connects concrete events to their route.
The jinn report a scripture that guides إلى الحق وإلى طريق مستقيم; the exact route language makes this a direct guidance parallel.
After Iblis promises to mislead people, God says “this is a straight path to Me”; it marks the boundary of the path Iblis cannot redefine. The wording of على has interpretive variation.
In the dispute over the direction of prayer, the verse says God guides whom He wills to a straight path; a changed direction makes the route's divine guidance concrete.
After people differ, God guides believers to the truth by His permission and guides whom He wills to a straight path; it links the path with resolving division.
People who reject the signs are described as deaf and dumb in darkness; God may leave one astray or place one on a straight path, a direct contrast of routes.
The signs are made clear so the way of criminals becomes distinct; the verse makes the wrong path recognizable by contrast.
Following most people would lead the hearer away from God's way because they follow conjecture; it warns that the well-trodden route can be the wrong one.
The covenant is followed by a warning that whoever disbelieves has strayed from سواء السبيل, the middle of the way named in the section's dictionary note.
The verse warns against following desires of people who strayed and led many astray from سواء السبيل; it combines losing the center with bad leadership.
The Messenger brings people from darkness into light and toward the path of the Mighty and Praiseworthy; this places the path within a journey toward a destination.
Moses and Aaron are commanded to remain upright and not follow the path of the ignorant; it directly joins steadfast walking with rejecting a divergent route.
Every community receives a messenger commanding worship of God and avoidance of false gods; some are guided and some deserve error, echoing the section's worship/path/straying sequence.
Abraham is grateful for God's favors, chosen, and guided to a straight path; this binds divine favor and the path as in the section's “those You favored.”
The Prophet is told to follow Abraham's way of worship; this makes a prior community's practiced way an example to follow.
The command to call people to God's way with wisdom stages the guide's act of showing a route to others.
The verse says Pharaoh أضل قومه وما هدى: he led his people astray and did not guide them, a direct reversal of the section's guide who goes ahead for a community.
Pharaoh claims, “I guide you only to the way of right guidance”; in its context this is a ruler's claim, exposing the danger of a false guide on the road.
A believer in Pharaoh's household says “follow me” and promises guidance to سبيل الرشاد; it stages a guide leading a community along a way.
Satanic companions turn people away from the way while their victims think they are guided; it shows false guidance as deviation masked as direction.
The verse says some recipients of scripture choose error and want others to stray from the way; it stages people trying to divert travelers from their route.
The regretful person wishes he had taken a way with the Messenger; 25:29 explains that a close companion led him away from the Reminder, so this verse contributes the lost communal route.
The speaker says his companion led him astray from the Reminder after it came; 25:27 names the abandoned way with the Messenger, and this verse identifies the misleading guide.
People in Hell say they obeyed their leaders and were led away from the way; this is a direct warning about following a community's guide in the wrong direction.
The verse states that the guided person benefits himself, while whoever strays bears it; the root ض ل ل named in the section is here contrasted with hidaya's outcome.
Thamud were shown guidance but preferred blindness over it; the verse presents a community rejecting the route made visible to them.
People turn back after guidance has become clear, and Satan makes this seem attractive; this is a specific reversal of staying on the guided road.
The prayer asks God not to let hearts deviate after guidance; it parallels the section's request to stay straight on a path already shown.
The community is commanded to hold together by God's rope and not disperse; this makes the section's contrast between a common road and people scattering in every direction concrete.
Those who split their religion and become factions are separated from the Prophet; this directly matches the section's dispersed groups as the opposite of a shared path.
The verse describes people who divided their religion into sects, each faction pleased with itself; it gives the section's “scattering in every direction” a communal form.
After 23:52 calls the community one, this verse says its people broke into factions; it contributes the specific fragmentation that opposes a shared road.
A connected chain of towns is set between Sheba and blessed towns, with travel measured between them; this places markers and repeated journeys along a route.

The people ask for longer distances between travel stops and are then scattered; 34:18 supplies the linked route, while this verse contributes the rejection of its connected stages and the resulting dispersion.
The people claim to be guided by following their fathers' آثار (traces); it contrasts inherited footprints with the section's path of those truly favored.
On the Day of Resurrection each people is called with its imam; this gives the section's path of a community a concrete image of groups gathered under a leader.
Moses asks to follow a teacher so he may learn right guidance; it stages the section's image of walking behind someone who knows the way.
Those who strive for God are promised guidance to His سبل, plural ways; the verse depicts sustained effort as the way into guidance.
Lut's people are accused of cutting off the road; this is a concrete obstruction to travel, reversing the section's passable, walked road.
The verse condemns those who block God's way and the Sacred Mosque; it directly stages a road being obstructed for others.
Those who disbelieve and bar people from God's way after guidance is clear are described as opposing the Messenger; it shows a known path deliberately blocked.
God promises believers a light by which they walk; this connects the section's wayfinding signs with actual movement along a route.
The Quran is said to guide to that which is most upright; it supplies a text as a guide toward the section's straightness, though without staging a physical road.

God makes the way easy for the human; this resonates specifically with the section's dictionary image of a road subdued by repeated walking, though السبيل here may mean life's way or the passage of birth.
The section reads ضالا فهدى as a seeker found and guided; because ضالًّا can be understood more broadly than losing a physical road, this is a qualified root-level reversal linking ض ل ل and ه د ي.
The source section's dictionary sense of مَلِك الطريق is the road's middle; this verse calls the Muslim community أمة وسطا, a centered community, though it is not literally describing a road.
The verse says God is على صراط مستقيم; this relates the section's straight path to the Lord's own just, steady course, not to a route humans physically walk.
The speakers say God has guided them to their ways and resolve to endure harm; it links received guidance with remaining on a route through difficulty.
The verse distinguishes the one God guides from the one He leaves astray; it directly connects the section's guidance/straying pair, though without a path scene.
Prophets are made leaders who guide by God's command; this parallels the section's guide who goes ahead of a community, while the verse names their leadership rather than a road.
Leaders among the people guide by God's command after patience; this gives a specific community-leading counterpart to the section's hâdî.
The verse says God guides to Himself whoever turns back to Him; it relates turning toward a destination to the section's guidance request, without describing a road.
The Prophet is commanded to invite people and remain upright as commanded; this connects calling others with steadfastness on the straight way.
The verse commands people to follow and calls that a straight path; its context identifies Jesus, so it adds a speaker-specific invitation to the path beside 43:64.

The verse continues the claim in 43:22 by showing earlier messengers met with the same appeal to ancestral practice; it gives the refusal context while 43:22 itself supplies the trace-following claim.
The verse says every people has a guide; this resonates with the section's hādī as a guide who goes before a group, though the verse does not describe the guide's route.
The verse describes people driven on their faces toward Hell and calls them most astray in path; it gives a bodily and destination-based reversal of the straight road.
Moses is told to travel by night and make a dry path through the sea for the Children of Israel; the verse turns the road into a passable route leading a whole people.
After Moses strikes the sea at God's command, it parts into towering sections; 20:77 names the dry path through it, and this verse contributes the opening that makes that route possible.
The regret in 25:27 continues with the speaker wishing he had not taken a particular person as a close companion; it contributes the choice of companion behind the wrong path described in 25:29.

The section names the secondary dictionary sense of دِين as a habitual way of acting; لكم دينكم ولي دين uses the same word for each side's religious way, but the link to repeated daily walking is interpretive rather than explicit.

The section's dictionary sense of هدى is showing someone the road and its destination; this verse marks a boundary on human guidance by saying the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, while God guides whom He wills.

The verse describes God bringing believers from darkness into light while unbelievers' patrons bring them from light into darkness; this is a specific reversal of the section's request for a guide toward the right way.
When Moses's people deviated, God made their hearts deviate; the verb زاغوا names turning away from the straight course, a direct boundary against remaining on it.
